evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a supplier says a non-price term matters especially to it DO offer that term conditionally in exchange for a specific improvement, and settle the exchanged terms together BECAUSE a concession the supplier values can motivate movement on a buyer priority; leaving it unresolved gives the supplier reason to hold its offer.
evidence.evidence: Supplier: “Faster payment would help us more than anything.” Later: “We really need to get the earlier payment terms agreed so we can wrap this up.”

evidence.lesson: [supplier_behaviour] WHEN a supplier cites a price-reduction freeze but also identifies negotiable commercial terms DO Test specific exchanges across those terms instead of treating the stated freeze as an end to negotiation. BECAUSE The supplier may still authorize a different package when it gains something it values, even while holding firm on price for the current terms.
evidence.evidence: SUPPLIER: “We can talk about the terms instead - payment, volume or contract length.”

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN the supplier says a non-price concession matters more to it than other terms DO make that concession conditional on a specific improvement in the terms that matter to the buyer BECAUSE the supplier indicated it would reflect the concession in its price, creating a trade rather than a one-sided give.
evidence.evidence: “Faster payment would help us more than anything. Faster payment is welcome; we can reflect it in the price.”

evidence.lesson: [supplier_behaviour] WHEN the supplier says a price freeze limits reductions but identifies terms it can trade DO test packages that change the terms the supplier values, rather than relying on a price request alone BECAUSE the supplier may be able to justify a concession through a valuable commitment even when it says base-price reductions are frozen
evidence.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “We can talk about the terms instead - payment, volume or contract length.”

tips.when: A supplier offers no additional benefit for a longer commitment
tips.action: Do not extend the commitment solely to seek a discount; look for a feasible change that would affect the offer.
tips.why: The buyer would give up flexibility without receiving value in return.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN the supplier says an additional concession in agreement length will not improve its price DO stop extending the commitment solely to seek a discount; ask which feasible change would actually affect the price BECAUSE a term that has stopped moving the supplier’s price gives away flexibility without closing the price gap
evidence.evidence: “To achieve further price improvements, an increase in the annual volume would be required.”

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN a supplier offers the same price for a longer and a shorter commitment DO do not give up flexibility for the longer commitment without a corresponding benefit BECAUSE the supplier gains stability, while the buyer receives no price saving for that concession.
evidence.evidence: “the longer agreement appears to carry the same price as your main offer.”

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN the supplier offers the same price for a shorter and a longer agreement DO Do not give the longer commitment without a compensating improvement; retain the shorter commitment if other terms are equal. BECAUSE A longer commitment costs flexibility, while identical prices provide no return for giving it.
evidence.evidence: “the quoted price remains the same for either term”

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN the supplier offers the same price for a longer commitment DO do not extend the agreement solely for a promised price benefit; ask for a distinct price step or keep the shorter commitment BECAUSE planning security benefits the supplier, but an unchanged price gives the buyer no saving in exchange for the added commitment
evidence.evidence: “Your latest offer keeps the same unit price for the longer term, so we would still need a price step for that commitment.”

tips.when: A supplier cites several cost indices to justify an increase without making their price impact clear
tips.action: Verify the cited movements and ask how the indices are weighted in its costs before assessing the increase.
tips.why: Headline movements cannot establish the price effect without their relative cost shares.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a supplier justifies a price increase with several cost indices DO check the underlying movements and ask how each index is weighted in the supplier’s costs, rather than adding the headline changes BECAUSE the price effect depends on each cost’s share; a weighted comparison can support a smaller, more defensible increase
evidence.evidence: “Your request for the figures behind our view is fair” and “We will send the published labour and energy sources and our weighting.”

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN the supplier justifies an increase with cost indices DO Check the cited movements against public data and challenge any part of the increase they do not explain. BECAUSE Verifiable contrary evidence can change the supplier’s calculation without requiring disclosure of its confidential costs.
evidence.evidence: “We checked the index change data you cited; it holds and we took it into account. We did not know that - a fair point.”

evidence.lesson: [supplier_behaviour] WHEN the supplier cites cost indices but rejects the buyer’s analysis of those same indices DO Ask how the claimed cost movements translate into the proposed base price, and distinguish that question from how future movements will be shared. BECAUSE Public indices alone did not persuade this supplier to reduce its base price; it treated its underlying cost structure and future material risk as separate reasons to hold firm.
evidence.evidence: “the public indices you referenced do not alter our underlying cost structure”; “we must maintain our price.”

tips.when: A supplier counters above a credible buyer proposal but continues reducing its price
tips.action: Consider holding the proposal for another round rather than improving it automatically.
tips.why: Another supplier concession may close the gap without the buyer giving up value.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a supplier counters above a buyer proposal but continues to reduce its price DO consider holding a credible proposal for another round rather than improving it automatically BECAUSE a further supplier concession may make the existing proposal acceptable without the buyer giving up more value
evidence.evidence: After another supplier e-mail saying “Our counter-offer,” the buyer repeated its package options unchanged; the supplier replied, “We agree.”

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN the supplier makes small price reductions after each higher buyer offer DO avoid repeatedly raising the buyer’s offer merely to obtain another small reduction; ask for a firmer supplier step before conceding again BECAUSE the supplier was responding to buyer concessions, so each higher offer gave away part of the remaining gap
evidence.evidence: “Thank you for your revised proposal; in response to your concession, we can lower our price.”

tips.when: Multiple suppliers quote and one provides a credible lower-priced benchmark
tips.action: Cite the competing offer accurately when asking higher-priced suppliers to revise their bids.
tips.why: A verifiable alternative can affect how far a supplier is willing to move.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN two or more suppliers quote and one offer provides a credible lower benchmark DO cite the competing offer when asking higher-priced suppliers to revise their bids BECAUSE suppliers may verify a rival quote and take it into account when deciding how far to move
evidence.evidence: “We checked the rival quote data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.”

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN another supplier has made a more competitive offer DO ask the preferred supplier to improve its price, using the competing offer as a credible alternative rather than accepting its opening quote BECAUSE Competition gives the supplier a reason to reconsider its price; accepting the opening quote captures no price concession.
evidence.evidence: The preferred supplier’s offer said, “Let us know if this works for you.” Its next e-mail was an order confirmation, with no intervening price concession.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a qualified competing quote is lower than a supplier’s offer DO cite the competing quote and ask the supplier to improve its offer BECAUSE the supplier may verify the quote and make an initial concession rather than lose the order
evidence.evidence: Back-office note: “The buyer shows a much lower rival quote. I give half the step now and check the rest.”

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a verified competing quote is materially lower than a supplier’s offer DO cite the competing quote and ask the supplier to improve its offer BECAUSE the supplier may treat credible competition as a reason to concede rather than dismissing the comparison
evidence.evidence: “We checked the rival quote data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.”

tips.when: A supplier proposes a quality commitment weaker than its verified past performance
tips.action: Cite the performance record and request a stronger commitment.
tips.why: An accepted record gives the supplier a concrete basis for revising the commitment.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN the supplier proposes a quality commitment that appears weaker than its recorded performance DO cite verified performance and ask for a stronger commitment BECAUSE a record the supplier accepts gives it a concrete basis for revising its offer rather than dismissing the request
evidence.evidence: “We checked the quality record data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.”

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a supplier's proposed quality commitment is weaker than the performance evidence in the case file DO cite the verified record and request a measurable, stronger commitment BECAUSE the supplier may check credible evidence and revise its quality offer rather than dismiss the request.
evidence.evidence: Supplier: “We checked the quality record data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.”

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN the case file contains a verified quality record that is stronger than the supplier’s proposed commitment DO cite the record and ask for a firmer quality commitment BECAUSE the supplier checked the evidence and used it when revising its offer.
evidence.evidence: “We checked the quality record data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.”

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a supplier's proposed quality commitment is weaker than its documented performance DO cite the performance record and request a firmer commitment as part of a package offer BECAUSE a verified record can make a stronger commitment credible even when the supplier resists a price cut
evidence.evidence: The supplier wrote, “We checked the quality record data you cited; it holds,” and then offered the buyer's requested quality commitment.

tips.when: A supplier seeks an index adjustment while its relevant costs remain covered at a fixed price
tips.action: Preserve fixed pricing through the covered period and seek a base-price concession before accepting later index risk.
tips.why: Deferral limits immediate exposure, but an index clause can still transfer future cost risk to the buyer.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN a supplier seeks an index adjustment despite having fixed-price material cover DO keep the price fixed through the covered period and require a meaningful base-price concession before accepting later index risk BECAUSE deferring the adjustment limits immediate exposure, but accepting the clause still transfers future cost risk to the buyer
evidence.evidence: “the index clause ... will apply after our fixed-price material cover ends”

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN the supplier says its input costs are covered at fixed prices and prefers a fixed-price agreement DO do not add an index clause merely to make an offer appear more attractive; seek a better fixed price first BECAUSE the clause shifts future price risk to the buyer without addressing the supplier’s stated need, and that risk reduces the value of the deal beyond its unit price.
evidence.evidence: “an index clause is not workable for us” and “We prefer to build on a fixed price agreement and can offer a further concession”

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN a supplier says an input is covered at fixed prices but offers an index clause tied to that input DO do not add the clause merely to obtain a lower starting price; weigh the future price risk against the discount BECAUSE An index can change the buyer’s later costs even when it does not track the supplier’s current cost exposure.
evidence.evidence: “an index would not accurately reflect our cost base. Therefore, we prefer to proceed with a fixed price”

tips.when: A supplier repeatedly counters on one of several buyer-proposed packages
tips.action: Treat that selection as evidence of its preferred terms and focus the next counter on improving that package.
tips.why: Repeated selection shows which combination the supplier is evaluating; revising unused alternatives may have little effect.

evidence.lesson: [supplier_behaviour] WHEN a supplier repeatedly counters on one of several offered packages DO treat that choice as evidence of its preferred terms and focus subsequent counters there BECAUSE repeated selection reveals which package the supplier is actually evaluating; revising unused alternatives may do little to move its price
evidence.evidence: “In response to your movement, we are reducing our price for Option B.”

evidence.lesson: [supplier_behaviour] WHEN a supplier repeatedly counters using the same option from a set of packages DO treat its chosen package as evidence of which terms it prefers, and focus the next counter on improving the price within that package BECAUSE Repeated selection is more informative than assuming the supplier values every proposed trade-off equally.
evidence.evidence: Supplier: “Building on your Option B” and, later, “Building on your Option B, we are prepared to make a further concession”.

evidence.lesson: [supplier_behaviour] WHEN a supplier repeatedly counters on price while keeping the same start date and payment terms DO Focus the next proposal on the price gap; do not assume alternative packages will change which terms the supplier prefers. BECAUSE In this exchange, the supplier repeatedly selected the package with its preferred timing and payment terms, then adjusted price in small steps.
evidence.evidence: “We are matching your step by reducing our price ... keeping the ... payment terms and ... start date.”

tips.when: A proposed price change conflicts with a documented contractual notice requirement
tips.action: Cite the contract and the notice calculation, then request revised terms.
tips.why: A verifiable contractual constraint can make the supplier reconsider its proposed change.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a proposed price change conflicts with a documented notice requirement DO cite the contract and the notice calculation, then ask for revised terms BECAUSE a verifiable contractual point can make the supplier reconsider its opening position
evidence.evidence: Buyer: “Our contract requires 90 days.” Supplier: “We checked the notice period data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.”

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a supplier proposes a price change that may conflict with the agreement’s notice requirements DO check the contract and challenge the proposed effective date with the relevant clause BECAUSE a verifiable contractual constraint gives the supplier a reason to revise its offer without dismissing its cost concerns
evidence.evidence: “We acknowledge your points regarding the contractual notice period and the energy index movements, which we have verified.”

tips.when: Offering a supplier a choice between packages that differ in price and complaint remedies
tips.action: Check whether each added remedy is worth its price premium before offering the choice.
tips.why: The supplier may choose the higher-priced package, so offering a choice does not itself protect the buyer’s saving.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN offering the supplier a choice among packages with the same quality commitment but different prices and complaint remedies DO check that the added remedy is worth its price premium to the buyer before inviting the supplier to choose BECAUSE the supplier can select the higher-priced package; giving it the choice does not ensure the buyer captures the greatest saving
evidence.evidence: The buyer wrote, “We can offer either of these packages - please choose the one that suits you better,” and the supplier accepted the package with the higher price and a complaint chargeback rather than the lower-priced package with the same quality commitment.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN a supplier prefers fewer complaint chargebacks in exchange for a lower price DO treat waived chargebacks as a concession and weigh the price reduction against the protection lost BECAUSE the supplier may accept the quality commitment while shifting complaint costs back to the buyer; savings are not measured by unit price alone
evidence.evidence: The buyer proposed “no per-complaint chargebacks in exchange for a lower price,” but the supplier replied that it could take that option only if “the price needs to be” higher than the buyer offered.

tips.when: A supplier attributes its price to rising costs and the buyer has a defensible cost analysis
tips.action: Present the analysis and use it to support a specific counteroffer.
tips.why: Cost evidence the supplier can check gives it a basis to reassess the price rather than treating the counteroffer as an unsupported target.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN the supplier justifies its quote with cost increases and the buyer has a defensible should-cost analysis DO cite the analysis and use it to support a concrete counteroffer BECAUSE the supplier may verify and take the buyer’s cost evidence into account rather than dismissing the counteroffer as an unsupported target
evidence.evidence: “We checked the should cost data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.”

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN the supplier justifies its quote with cost pressures and the buyer has a credible cost estimate DO present the estimate and ask the supplier to check it, then use the response to support a revised offer BECAUSE a verified estimate gives the buyer's price request a factual basis, though it may not overcome the supplier's other constraints by itself
evidence.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “We checked the should cost data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.”

tips.when: A supplier says a cited cost index has little effect on its own costs
tips.action: Do not keep relying on that index for a price reduction; seek more relevant cost evidence or a different trade
tips.why: An index movement offers little leverage if it has little effect on the supplier’s pricing decision.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN the supplier says a cited cost index has little effect on its own costs DO do not keep relying on that index for a further price reduction; seek evidence tied more closely to its costs or change the proposed trade BECAUSE a valid index does not create bargaining leverage if the supplier sees little margin impact.
evidence.evidence: “We checked the energy index data you cited; it holds, but the impact on our side is tiny.”

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN a supplier verifies a cost-index change but says that index has little effect on its costs DO do not rely on that index alone to justify a further price cut; look for evidence tied to the supplier's main cost drivers BECAUSE a valid index movement has limited negotiating force if it represents little of the supplier's cost base
evidence.evidence: The supplier wrote, “we checked the energy index data you cited; it holds, but it barely affects our actual costs,” and identified other main cost drivers.

tips.when: A supplier requests proof of competing bids that the buyer cannot provide or disclose
tips.action: Do not rely on an unsupported competition claim or reveal confidential quotations; state the commercial target and negotiate the available terms.
tips.why: A supplier may discount an unverifiable claim while still considering a concrete commercial proposal.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN a supplier asks for proof after the buyer invokes competing bids DO Do not rely on an unsupported competition claim or disclose confidential quotations; state the commercial target and continue negotiating the available terms. BECAUSE A supplier that cannot verify the claimed competition may refuse to reduce its price on that basis.
evidence.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “if you can't show me the competition's prices, I can't just drop mine.”

tips.when: A supplier seeks an increase during a fixed-price period
tips.action: Negotiate the effective date as well as the price.
tips.why: Delaying an increase can preserve value even if some later price correction is needed.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN the supplier seeks an increase during a fixed-price period DO negotiate the effective date as well as the price rather than treating the requested start date as fixed BECAUSE delaying an increase can preserve value even when some price correction is needed
evidence.evidence: Buyer: “The fixed-price clause rules out your proposed November increase.” The supplier later offered a price “valid from 1 April 2027.”

tips.when: A supplier counters above the buyer’s latest price proposal while leaving other terms unchanged
tips.action: Consider one more specific price request before accepting.
tips.why: The remaining gap may still be negotiable, while immediate acceptance gives up that potential saving.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN the supplier counters above the buyer’s latest offer while keeping the other terms unchanged DO do not accept automatically; consider a final, smaller price request before closing BECAUSE an unchanged package leaves a clear price gap, and accepting immediately gives up any remaining negotiable saving
evidence.evidence: Buyer offered “EUR 136.22 per unit” with the proposed payment terms and effective date; the supplier countered at “€136.80 per unit while keeping payment” on those terms.

tips.when: A supplier justifies its price with a volatile input-cost index
tips.action: Consider trading a symmetric index adjustment for a lower fixed component of the price, and assess the resulting risk.
tips.why: Sharing future cost movements may support a lower starting price but transfers some price risk to the buyer.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a supplier justifies its price with a volatile input-cost index DO consider a symmetric index clause as a trade for a lower fixed component of the price, while assessing the resulting price risk BECAUSE sharing future cost movements can make a lower starting price acceptable to the supplier, but shifts some risk back to the buyer
evidence.evidence: Supplier e-mail: “to share the material risk, as you suggested.” The supplier then wrote: “We can accept your terms and await your order.”

tips.when: A supplier attributes its price to stock allocation or service commitments
tips.action: Identify the services the buyer needs and request a separately priced, reduced-service alternative.
tips.why: Reducing a clearly defined obligation may lower the supplier’s cost while making the buyer’s service trade-off visible.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a supplier attributes a price difference to stock allocation or service levels DO Specify which services the buyer needs and ask for a separately priced, reduced-service alternative before treating the item as a simple stock purchase. BECAUSE The supplier says those commitments carry costs. A clearly reduced scope gives it a reason to change its quote while making the quality trade-off visible.
evidence.evidence: “The difference between list and renewal quotes accounts for dedicated stock allocations and specific service levels.”

tips.when: A supplier proposes specification changes as a source of savings
tips.action: Keep those savings separate from the current deal until the changes receive the necessary technical approval.
tips.why: A cheaper offer based on unapproved specifications may be unusable or compromise quality.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN the supplier proposes specification changes as a source of savings DO keep those savings separate from the deal under negotiation until the appropriate technical approval is secured BECAUSE a cheaper quote based on unapproved changes may sacrifice quality or prove unusable
evidence.evidence: “The drawing changes you suggest would also need engineering approval.”

tips.when: A proposed increase conflicts with both a contractual requirement and a favorable demand forecast
tips.action: Cite the relevant records and ask the supplier to account for both in a revised offer.
tips.why: Verifiable contract and demand information can change the supplier’s assessment of the proposed increase.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN the supplier proposes a price increase despite a contractual notice requirement or a favorable demand forecast DO cite the relevant contract and forecast records, and ask the supplier to reflect both in a revised offer BECAUSE The supplier checked these facts, acknowledged them, and used the forecast to revise its calculation.
evidence.evidence: Supplier: “We also checked the notice period data you cited; it holds and we took it into account. We did not know that - a fair point. We have also taken your positive volume forecast into account, which allows us to adjust our calculation.”

tips.when: A supplier holds its price but remains willing to discuss other terms
tips.action: Negotiate valuable non-price terms explicitly rather than treating the price hold as the end of bargaining.
tips.why: The supplier may have room to change obligations or service terms while protecting its price.

evidence.lesson: [supplier_behaviour] WHEN the supplier holds its price but continues discussing other terms DO negotiate each valuable term explicitly rather than treating a price hold as the end of bargaining BECAUSE the supplier may still trade on non-price terms while protecting its price
evidence.evidence: Back-office notes: “My call: hold.” A later e-mail said, “we can step up to” a stronger quality commitment.

tips.when: Verified contractual or service-performance records reveal a discrepancy relevant to a supplier’s proposed price
tips.action: Identify the specific discrepancy and ask the supplier to account for it in a revised offer.
tips.why: Records the supplier can check may expose an assumption it omitted from its pricing assessment.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN the case file contains verifiable notice requirements or delivery performance that bears on the offer DO Cite the specific discrepancy when requesting a better price. BECAUSE The supplier acknowledged facts it had not accounted for and adjusted its offer rather than dismissing the request.
evidence.evidence: Supplier: “As to the index change and notice period data you cited, we did not know that - a fair point.” On delivery data: “I have adjusted our price to reflect this verified data.”

tips.when: Several suppliers have been asked to quote and the buyer has not yet committed to an order
tips.action: Compare their complete offers before confirming an order.
tips.why: Committing before comparing bids can forfeit a better offer and the leverage it provides.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN several suppliers have been asked to quote and an order has not yet been confirmed DO compare their offers before accepting one BECAUSE Confirming an order ends the opportunity to use a more competitive offer as leverage.
evidence.evidence: The first supplier replied, “Thank you for your order. Our order confirmation is attached.” Other supplier offers also appear in the e-mail record.

tips.when: A supplier repeatedly says a lead-time requirement is necessary for its production schedule
tips.action: Treat that lead time as a likely constraint and seek value through feasible price or other terms instead of repeatedly demanding a shorter lead time.
tips.why: The supplier may have room to improve the deal while being unable to change its schedule.

evidence.lesson: [supplier_behaviour] WHEN a supplier repeatedly describes a lead-time requirement as necessary for its production schedule DO treat that lead time as a likely constraint and seek value on feasible terms instead of making a shorter lead time central to every proposal BECAUSE the supplier may make price concessions while holding its scheduling requirement fixed
evidence.evidence: “The lead time is strictly necessary given our current capacity utilisation.” Later: “The lead time remains a strict requirement for our production scheduling.”

tips.when: The buyer wants to use the claimed cost of its concession as leverage
tips.action: Check that the claimed cost is supportable before citing it; otherwise describe the concession without overstating its value.
tips.why: A supplier can challenge an unsupported claim, weakening the case for a reciprocal improvement.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN claiming that a concession is costly without figures to support it DO verify its value before using it as leverage; otherwise describe the concession without overstating it BECAUSE the supplier can challenge an unsupported claim, weakening the buyer's case for a reciprocal concession.
evidence.evidence: Supplier: “can you send over the numbers to back that up?” Buyer: “We cannot substantiate that description with complaint-cost data, so we withdraw it.”

tips.when: A supplier has quoted standard terms but has not indicated which trade-offs it values
tips.action: Offer clearly priced alternative packages that vary commercial terms alongside price.
tips.why: The supplier’s response can reveal which terms support a better offer, giving the buyer a basis for the next counter.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN the supplier has quoted standard terms and has not yet revealed which trade-offs matter most DO Offer alternative packages that exchange price for contract length, payment terms, or price protection. BECAUSE The alternatives can elicit a lower quote while revealing which conditions the supplier needs to make it.
evidence.evidence: “We have reviewed your offer and can adjust our Angebot as follows.”

tips.when: Offering a supplier alternative packages with identical non-price terms
tips.action: Do not include a higher-priced package unless it gives the buyer a distinct benefit.
tips.why: The supplier can counter from the higher price without giving the buyer anything in return.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN two buyer packages give the supplier the same non-price terms DO Do not offer a higher price in one package without receiving a distinct benefit in return. BECAUSE The supplier can use the higher-priced package as the basis for its counteroffer, weakening the lower-priced request.
evidence.evidence: Buyer: “Option A is the leaner fixed-price route.” The two fixed-price packages had the same other terms. Supplier: “Building on your Option B” when countering from the higher-priced package.

tips.when: A supplier accepts the buyer’s proposed timing but counters above the buyer’s proposed price
tips.action: Treat timing as partial agreement and assess the remaining price gap before accepting.
tips.why: Agreement on one term does not mean the full package—or its potential saving—has been secured.

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN the supplier counters above a buyer-proposed price while adopting the buyer's proposed timing DO do not treat agreement on timing as full acceptance of the package; evaluate the remaining price gap before accepting BECAUSE A supplier can build on one option without accepting all its terms. Here the deal closed after that counter, while the result captured only part of the possible saving.
evidence.evidence: Supplier: “Building on your third option, we propose a revised price of EUR 136.30 per unit for this later effective date.” Result: “score 0.56.”

tips.when: A supplier negotiator says a requested concession exceeds their authority
tips.action: Keep a credible, specific request open while allowing time for internal approval.
tips.why: An approver may authorize a further concession that the negotiator cannot offer immediately.

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a supplier says a concession exceeds the negotiator’s authority DO Keep a credible, specific request on the table while allowing time for internal approval. BECAUSE The negotiator may have room to improve the offer after an approver authorises a further step.
evidence.evidence: Back-office notes: “The buyer wants more than my band allows. Approve a further step?” and “Approved: you may go further, within our rules.”

evidence.lesson: [do] WHEN a supplier representative says the requested concession exceeds their authority DO give the representative a specific revised package to take to an internal decision-maker, rather than treating their current offer as final BECAUSE the representative may need approval for a further concession; their stated limit is not necessarily the supplier’s limit
evidence.evidence: Back-office note: “The buyer wants more than my band allows. Approve a further step?”

evidence.lesson: [avoid] WHEN a supplier says it still needs to review its price internally DO do not place the order before following up on that review BECAUSE accepting immediately closes the negotiation while a further price decision may still be pending
evidence.evidence: “We need to clarify this internally - we will come back to you on price.” The next supplier message was: “Thank you for your order. Our order confirmation is attached.”
